title: Family furious after first day of coroner's inquest
article: The first day of the Clay Willey custody death inquest has upset members of Willey's family. Although they pressed for the inquest to take place, testimony of the beating Willey received at the hands of the RCMP and descriptions of the autopsy had some family and friends visibly shaken in the gallery and angry outside the coroner's office.

"It's horrible. It's hard to sit through lies," said Willey's friend Monique Gonyou. "I think a lot of what the pathologist was saying was put in his mouth by the RCMP. He (Willey) had been clean for the past five months and the one time he slips up is the day he died."

Willey's mother was likewise upset, especially about a moment of cross-examination by their lawyer, Dan Weatherly, of pathologist Dr. James McNaughton. Weatherly asked him about a missing molar and what would have caused it. McNaughton responded that indeed teeth were missing, including the molar, but he was unable to determine when it might have been dislodged. There was no corresponding facial injury to indicate the tooth was lost during the fight with police.
"The nurse at the hospital told us the bleeding in his mouth was from the teeth they knocked out," said Willey's mother Gloria.

Willey's girlfriend Miranda Savard, mother of Clay Alvin Willey Jr. who was not yet born at the time of his father's death, says she doesn't believe cocaine makes someone behave the way Willey did that night, and the police are trying to cover up their actions. "It has taken us a long time to get this inquest to happen, and hopefully the truth will come out," she said.

Willey's sister Bryna goes a step further in her finger-pointing at the RCMP. "There were times Clayton had been told by the police that they were going to get him. Going to kill him," Bryna said. "He feared the police. He paid people to walk with him to feel safer. He died in the way he most feared."

The financial burden on the Willey family and their supporters is the reason a trust account has been set up at Scotiabank for donations to offset legal costs. Willey family friend Yvonne Shuman says the legal bills are mounting and they didn't have the financial wherewithal to have their side properly represented by expert witnesses.

"We couldn't afford to have our own pathologist do an autopsy," she said. "Today on the stand, this pathologist (McNaughton) admitted this was the first time he had done an autopsy involving a Taser gun. How do you know how to examine for something you don't know about? The RCMP went and sent out a news release saying the cause of death was cocaine even before the family knew a report had been released. I'm nauseated by this, but I'm not surprised at the way things are coming out, because that is how they interpreted what happened."

The Prince George RCMP responded by saying the coroner's inquest was a process they have to sit through just like the rest of the public, and at the end they will implement whatever recommendations the inquest produces.

"The RCMP welcomes the coroner's inquest," said RCMP media communications officer Const. Gary Godwin. "It is a fact-finding process that allows for a full disclosure of the facts. We welcome the opportunity to describe our actions, as pertains to this particular case. The inquest is a forum that allows us to disclose our investigative steps, finding for the ultimate goal of ensuring that we are providing the best possible police services to the communities we police."
The inquest is scheduled to run for about two weeks.
